terms.means: Zero, when giving a football score. 2-0 is said 'two-nil'.
terms.use: Two-nil, and honestly it should've been more.

terms.means: A game where your side doesn't let in a goal.
terms.use: Scrappy, but we kept a clean sheet, so I'm happy.

terms.means: Three goals by the same player in one match. He gets to keep the match ball.
terms.use: First hat-trick I've seen live in years.

terms.means: Two goals by the same player in one match.
terms.use: Bagged a brace and he's not even our main striker.

terms.means: A world-class goal, usually a long-range strike.
terms.use: Their keeper had no chance. Absolute worldie.

terms.means: A thumping shot from distance that flies in.
terms.use: Came out of nowhere, a screamer from thirty yards.

terms.means: The top corners of the goal. A shot in there is near impossible to save.
terms.use: One touch to set himself and he put it top bins.

terms.means: An easy chance that gets missed.
terms.use: How do you miss that from two yards? Total sitter.

terms.means: A glaring, often comical mistake, usually by a goalkeeper or the ref.
terms.use: Their keeper's had a howler. Went straight through his hands.

terms.means: A very easy goal from right in front of the net.
terms.use: Not pretty, just a tap-in, but they all count.

terms.means: Knocking the ball through an opponent's legs and collecting it on the other side.
terms.use: He nutmegged their centre-back and the whole ground went up.

terms.means: Short for a penalty.
terms.use: That's a pen all day long.

terms.means: A penalty beyond any argument. Strangely, 'stonewall' here means 'certain'.
terms.use: Stonewall pen, and somehow the ref waved it away.

terms.means: A penalty given for very little contact.
terms.use: Bit of a soft pen, but I'll take it.

terms.means: The manager. An informal British word for the boss.
terms.use: The gaffer's got to change something at half-time.

terms.means: To lose your nerve and throw away a winning position. Someone who does it is a 'bottler'. Having 'bottle' means having nerve.
terms.use: Two up at half-time and we still bottled it.

terms.means: The early stages of a match.
terms.use: We needed a goal early doors to settle the nerves.

terms.means: When a team puts everyone behind the ball and just defends.
terms.use: They came here, parked the bus and dared us to break them down.

terms.means: A match against a side near you in the table. Win and you gain three while they miss out on three.
terms.use: Proper six-pointer this weekend. We can't lose it.

terms.means: The tense final stretch of a season or a match.
terms.use: Five games left and it's tight. Squeaky bum time.

terms.means: Relegation to the division below.
terms.use: Couple more wins and we're clear of the drop.

terms.means: Pinned back under heavy, sustained pressure from the other side.
terms.use: We were under the cosh for the last twenty minutes.

terms.means: A win nicked by a side that was outplayed for most of the game.
terms.use: Total smash and grab. Barely had a shot and we won.

terms.means: To escape with a result you didn't really deserve.
terms.use: We got out of jail there, no question.

terms.means: Players squaring up and shoving each other without any real fighting.
terms.use: Bit of handbags after the tackle, nothing in it.

terms.means: The back row of the stand. Putting the ball 'into Row Z' means clearing it as far as possible.
terms.use: Don't mess about with it, just stick it in Row Z.

terms.means: To boot the ball long and aimlessly instead of passing it.
terms.use: All we did second half was hoof it up to the big man.

terms.means: A match against your local rivals.
terms.use: Forget the table, it's derby week.

terms.means: The right to wind up the losing side's fans until the next meeting.
terms.use: It's not about the points, it's bragging rights at work on Monday.

terms.means: Being sent off. The player heads for the changing room before everyone else.
terms.use: Two silly yellows and he's off for an early bath.

terms.means: The posts and crossbar.
terms.use: Hit the woodwork twice and still couldn't score.

terms.means: A match with nothing riding on it because the outcome is already settled.
terms.use: It's a dead rubber, so let's see some of the youngsters.

terms.means: When a defender keeps a forward completely quiet all game.
terms.use: Our centre-half had him in his pocket all afternoon.

terms.means: Played really badly.
terms.use: Our left-back had a shocker. Got skinned every time.

terms.means: A goal scored by the side that was being outplayed at the time.
terms.use: Their goal came totally against the run of play.

open.m: The safest opener there is. Let them tell you how it went.

open.t: What did you make of the weekend, then?
open.m: Open question. Works whether your side won, lost or drew.
Use on a matchday. Shows you know there's a game on.

open.t: How are your lot getting on?
open.m: Asks about their team. 'Your lot' is friendly shorthand for their club.
Vague but sounds clued up. Nearly every weekend is a big one for someone.
Invites them to talk about league positions, good or bad.

open.t: Still not over Saturday, to be honest.
open.m: Hints at a dramatic result without saying what. They'll fill in the gaps.

open.t: You going to the game or watching it down the pub?
open.m: Natural matchday question. Either answer gets them talking.

opinion.t: We need a proper striker, simple as.
opinion.m: Nearly every fan thinks this, whatever the results.

opinion.t: Midfield's the problem. Always has been.
opinion.m: Hard to argue with, and nobody can prove you wrong.

opinion.t: We're a different side at home.
opinion.m: A common observation most fans will nod along to.
Sounds wise. Works whether you're near the top or the bottom.

opinion.t: We're too easy to play against.
opinion.m: A favourite complaint about a side that lacks fight.

opinion.t: We give the ball away far too cheaply.
opinion.m: Fair criticism of almost any team.

opinion.t: We can't defend a corner to save our lives.
opinion.m: A classic gripe about set pieces. Fits most sides at some point.

opinion.t: We've got to get a few bodies in next window.
opinion.m: The transfer window is when clubs can sign players. Most fans think the squad is too thin.

agree.m: Short and firm. They'll carry on talking.
Sympathetic. Invites them to say more.
Makes it sound like you've thought this for weeks.
Plain agreement that hands the floor back.
Agrees while nudging them to explain more.
Works for any grumble about your own team.
Strong agreement. They'll usually repeat it and add more.

dodge.m: Sounds like you've got loads to say. Let them do the talking.

dodge.t: I'm trying not to think about it, to be honest.
dodge.m: Works after good or bad results and moves things on.

dodge.t: Ask me again after the weekend.
I've given up trying to predict this lot.

dodge.m: Safe on anything about the season.

dodge.t: Let's see where we are in a month.
Never mind us, how are your lot doing?
dodge.m: Turns it round so they talk about their team instead.

telly.m: When a player dithers on the edge of the box.
When the other side gets a penalty you don't agree with.
When your defenders dawdle on the ball near their own goal.
Warning your player someone's closing in behind. Players shout it on the pitch too.
When your defender dives into a tackle and risks giving away a foul.

exit.t: Right, I'd better get back to it.
exit.m: Office classic. Ends things without any fuss.

exit.t: Anyway, we'll see what happens at the weekend.
exit.m: A sign-off that works almost any week of the season.

exit.t: Can't stand here talking football all day.
Anyway, I'm off. Enjoy the game.
Let's catch up after the next one.
exit.m: Polite, and implies you'll be watching.
In the pub, the perfect change of subject.
Pub-friendly sign-off that suggests you'll be back.

win.them: Not bad. Wasn't exactly pretty though, was it?
win.back: Don't care. Three points is three points.
win.agree: Fair enough, a win's a win.
win.exit: Exactly. Right, I'll let you get on.

bigWin.them: Yeah, {opp} didn't turn up at all, did they?
bigWin.back: Maybe not, but you can only beat what's in front of you.
bigWin.agree: True. Goal difference will thank you later.
bigWin.exit: Let's not get carried away. Back down to earth next week, probably.

narrowWin.them: Last ten minutes must have been nervy.
narrowWin.back: I was watching through my fingers. But we got the job done.
narrowWin.agree: Those are the ones that matter come the end of the season.
narrowWin.exit: Hope so. My heart rate's only just back to normal. Catch you later.

draw.open: {score} with {opp} {when}. Can't decide if that's a point gained or two dropped.
draw.them: Depends who you ask, doesn't it?
draw.back: We had the chances to win it. That's what annoys me.
draw.agree: Yeah, feels like one that got away.
draw.exit: Ah well, onto the next one.

goallessDraw.open: Nil-nil {when}. Not one for the highlights.
goallessDraw.back: Dire's being kind. Still, a clean sheet's something.
goallessDraw.agree: Yeah, at least the back line held up.
goallessDraw.exit: I'll have forgotten it by the weekend. See you later.

loss.back: {opp} wanted it more, simple as. We never got going.
loss.agree: It happens. Every side has off days.
loss.exit: Yeah. Let's change the subject before I get wound up.

bigLoss.open: {score}. Go on, get it out of your system.
bigLoss.back: Embarrassing. Some of that lot owe the fans an apology.
bigLoss.agree: Fair. Not good enough at any level, that.
bigLoss.exit: I'm not watching the highlights. Right, I'm off before I start ranting again.

lateWinner.open: Last-minute winner {when}! I've still got no voice.
lateWinner.them: {player} at the death, wasn't it? Brilliant.
lateWinner.back: Right at the death. Best feeling in football, that.
lateWinner.exit: I'll be watching it back all week. Catch you later.

lateConcede.open: Ninety minutes of hard work {when} and we throw it away at the death.
lateConcede.back: Everyone. We sat too deep and invited {opp} on.
lateConcede.agree: Yeah, you can't keep dropping off like that.
lateConcede.exit: Don't remind me. I'll be stewing on it all week.

comeback.open: Went behind {when} and still won it {score}. What a game.
comeback.them: Didn't see that coming when you went a goal down.
comeback.back: Nor did I. But the lads showed a bit of bottle for once.
comeback.exit: Feel like I've earned a pint just watching it. Speak soon.

blewLead.open: We were cruising {when}, and somehow we threw it away.
blewLead.back: Completely. Got comfortable, stopped running and let {opp} back in.
blewLead.agree: Classic. It's never won till the final whistle.
blewLead.exit: Lesson learned, hopefully. I'll believe it when I see it.

redCardLoss.open: Down to ten men {when} and it all fell apart.
redCardLoss.back: Soft, but he gave the ref a decision to make. Daft challenge.
redCardLoss.agree: Yeah, you can't leave yourselves short like that.
redCardLoss.exit: And now he's suspended as well. Anyway, I'd better crack on.

cleanSheetWin.them: Defence looked solid, by all accounts.
cleanSheetWin.back: Didn't give {opp} a sniff all game.
cleanSheetWin.exit: Let's hope they keep it up. Right, back to work.

hatTrickWin.open: Hat-trick for {player} {when}! He's taking the match ball home.
hatTrickWin.them: Yeah, I saw. He was on fire.
hatTrickWin.back: Every time he got near the box you thought he'd score.
hatTrickWin.agree: Hope he keeps that form going.
hatTrickWin.exit: Don't jinx it. Anyway, catch you later.

possessionLoss.open: Had most of the ball {when} and still lost to {opp}. Typical.
possessionLoss.them: Lot of passing sideways, was it?
possessionLoss.back: Exactly. No end product. {opp} barely had a kick and nicked it.
possessionLoss.agree: Possession counts for nothing if you don't hurt them.
possessionLoss.exit: Tell that to our midfield. Anyway, I'm off.

derbyWin.open: Beat {opp} {when}. I'm going to be unbearable all week.
derbyWin.them: I'd expect nothing less. Their lot have gone very quiet.
derbyWin.back: Bragging rights are ours. I'll be reminding a few people at work.
derbyWin.agree: Fair play, that's what derbies are all about.
derbyWin.exit: Right, I'm off to find someone in the other colours. See you.

derbyLoss.open: Lost to {opp} {when}. Of all the teams.
derbyLoss.them: Derby defeat? You'll be keeping your head down at work, then.
derbyLoss.back: Taking the long way round to the kettle all week, yeah.
derbyLoss.exit: We'll get them next time. Right, I'll leave it there.

pub.say: Ref was a joke tonight, wasn't he?
o: Shocking. He was giving them everything.
Takes your mate's side and keeps the moan going.
Over a season, refereeing errors tend to even out statistically.
Probably true, but nobody wants a lecture at the bar.
Which one was the referee?
Instant giveaway. The ref's the one everyone's been shouting at.

pub.say: We're going down this year, I'm telling you.
o: Down where?
'Going down' means relegation, and everyone in the pub knows it.
Don't be daft. There's plenty worse than us.
Fans moan, and mates talk each other round.
Our points per game projects to a comfortable mid-table finish.
Sounds like a spreadsheet, not a mate.

pub.say: What a goal. Right in the top bins.
o: A superb strike with excellent technique.
Accurate, but it sounds like a coaching manual.
What's a top bin?
Top bins are the top corners of the goal. Fans say it all the time.
Unstoppable. Keeper never even moved.
Matches their excitement and paints the right picture.
Go on then, I'm in.
Simple, keen and natural.
Is that the soccer?
It's football in Britain. 'Soccer' marks you out straight away.
Certainly. What time is kick-off scheduled for?
Fine question, but stiff and formal for a pub.
Low-scoring games often reflect two well-organised defensive structures.
Analytical and dull when your mate wanted sympathy.
Worst ninety minutes of my life. Clean sheet, mind.
Moans like a fan, then finds the one bright side.
So it was a tie at zero?
In Britain it's a draw, and the score is nil-nil.
Did he get injured?
'Had a shocker' means he played badly, not that he got hurt.
His save percentage was well below his season average.
Too much like reading out a stats sheet.
Proper howler. Fumbling everything.
Agrees and uses the word fans reach for.
Massive. Lose that and we're in real trouble.
Shows you know what's riding on it.
Six points? I thought a win was worth three.
A six-pointer is against a side near you in the table, so the swing counts double.
Yes, a direct contest with a club in close proximity in the league table.
Correct, but nobody talks like that over a pint.
Under the Laws of the Game, contact alone isn't necessarily a foul.
Technically right, but it kills the moment.
Never a what?
'Pen' is short for penalty. Fans use it constantly.
Not in a million years. He went down far too easily.
Backs your mate up and sounds like you watched it.

avoid.why: In Britain it's football. 'Soccer' sounds American, even though the word started in England.
Football scores use 'nil' for zero: nil-nil, one-nil, two-nil.
A team's shirt, shorts and socks are its kit. 'Uniform' is for American sports or school.
British fans play and watch on a pitch.
Footballers wear boots. The grips underneath are studs.
A level result is a draw. In British football a 'tie' usually means a cup match.
Not conceding is keeping a clean sheet. 'Shutout' is North American.
The extra half-hour in a cup game is extra time. Minutes added on at the end of a half are stoppage time.
Fans talk about where they are in the table, or the league table.
In Britain 'derby' starts like 'dark'. The American 'DER-bee' stands out.

nerd: If you look at our expected-goals difference over the last six, we're running about nought-point-four per ninety below the underlying numbers, so results should regress upwards.
offq: Who'd you play at left-back if the first-choice lad gets injured?
unsure: sources: BBC Sport, The Guardian and The Athletic block this research tool, so none could be read directly. Terms were cross-checked against Wikipedia, Goal, AP (via WTOP), Sky Sports, the Premier League site, OUP and dictionaries instead.
sources: FourFourTwo's glossary page would not load past its title. Only its origins article's headline and search summary (bottle, early doors, handbags) were used.
sources: the Premier League has no general fan glossary; only its 'Premier League explained' page and the Fantasy Premier League help page were used.
megs / megged (for nutmeg): Wikipedia lists it for Ireland, Australia and New Zealand; could not confirm it as standard UK usage, so left out.
lino (for linesman): no reliable source found, so left out.
scenes (for wild celebrations): could not confirm in a reliable source, so left out.
had a shocker: confirmed for a player's bad game; using it for referees is common but only backed by a learner site, so the term's example sticks to a player.
the drop: backed by football glossaries and press usage, but there is no standard dictionary entry.
get out of jail: backed by a learner site and match-report usage, no dictionary entry.
telly line 'That's never a pen!': ordinary British phrasing ('never' meaning 'definitely not'); no glossary lists it as a set phrase.
early doors: origin is disputed (theatre entry vs pub opening times), so only the meaning is given.
tie: the note that a British 'tie' usually means a cup match is from general knowledge of usage; sources only confirmed draw vs tie as a UK/US difference.
